title: Sleep and Screens
summary: Why children need nine to twelve hours of sleep, how light from screens confuses the body's inner clock and melatonin, and what bedtime habits help everyone sleep better.
poll: Using a phone or tablet in bed is fine as long as you turn it off before you fall asleep.

versions.title: Sleep and Screens
versions.text:
It is late. You are in bed. But you have a game on a screen. You play one more round. Then one more. Now it is very late!

Sleep is not lost time. It is when your body rests and grows. Your brain is busy too. It sorts what you learned that day. It helps you keep it.

Kids need lots of sleep. Most need nine to twelve hours each night. That is a lot!

Your body has a clock. It knows day from night by light. When it gets dark, your brain makes you feel sleepy.

But a screen gives off bright light. The light can fool your brain. It thinks it is still day. So you do not feel sleepy. Games and clips can keep you wide awake, too.

Then you wake up tired. It is hard to think in class. You may feel grumpy.

So make a good habit. Turn off screens an hour or so before bed. Read a book. Keep your room dark. Then sleep well!

versions.title: Sleep and Screens
versions.text:
It is late at night, and you are lying in bed with a tablet. A colorful game glows on the screen, and you promise yourself just one more round. Then you play another, and another, until you suddenly realize that it is nearly midnight and your alarm will ring in only a few hours.

Many people consider sleep to be wasted time, but it is actually one of the most productive periods for the human body. During deep sleep, the body releases a growth hormone, repairs damaged tissues, and restores its energy. The brain remains remarkably active as well, organizing the information it absorbed during the day and consolidating it into long-lasting memories. Adequate sleep also strengthens the immune system, which helps the body defend itself against infections.

Children require a considerable amount of sleep, and health experts recommend that most children between six and twelve years old get nine to twelve hours every night.

The body also contains an internal clock, called the circadian rhythm, which relies on light to distinguish day from night. When darkness falls, the brain releases a hormone called melatonin, which gradually makes a person feel drowsy.

Screens, however, emit bright light, including a type known as blue light. This light can deceive the brain into behaving as if it were still daytime, so it produces less melatonin and the person remains alert. Exciting games, videos, and notifications can also keep the mind racing long after the lights go out. Some devices offer a night mode that reduces blue light, which may help slightly, but researchers point out that stimulating content can still keep the brain awake.

The following morning, a tired student may find it more difficult to concentrate during lessons, may forget important information, and may feel irritable with friends and family.

For these reasons, it is helpful to establish a healthy and consistent bedtime routine. Switch off every device approximately an hour before bed and read a paper book instead, keep the bedroom dark and quiet, charge phones outside the room, and go to sleep at the same time each night.

Many people regard sleep as unproductive time, but it is actually one of the most essential periods for the human body. During deep sleep, the body releases a growth hormone, repairs damaged tissues, and replenishes its energy supplies. The brain remains remarkably active as well, systematically organizing the information it absorbed throughout the day and consolidating it into durable memories that can be retrieved later. Adequate sleep additionally strengthens the immune system, which enables the body to defend itself more effectively against infections.

Children require a considerable amount of sleep, and pediatric health experts recommend that most children between six and twelve years old obtain nine to twelve hours every night, although individual requirements vary somewhat from one child to another.

The body also contains an internal timekeeping system, known as the circadian rhythm, which depends on environmental light to distinguish day from night. When darkness falls, the brain secretes a hormone called melatonin, which gradually induces drowsiness and prepares the body for restorative sleep.

Electronic screens, however, emit intense artificial light, including a variety known as blue light, which can deceive the brain into behaving as if it were still daytime. Consequently, the brain manufactures less melatonin, and the individual remains alert. Stimulating games, videos, and continual notifications can additionally keep the mind racing long after the lights have been extinguished. Although numerous devices now incorporate a night mode that reduces blue light, researchers emphasize that captivating content can nevertheless keep the brain overstimulated.

The following morning, a sleep-deprived student may find it considerably more difficult to concentrate during lessons, may struggle to recall important information, and may feel unusually irritable with friends and family members.

For these reasons, specialists recommend establishing a healthy and consistent bedtime routine: switching off every electronic device approximately an hour before bed, reading a paper book instead, keeping the bedroom dark and quiet, charging phones outside the room, and going to sleep at the same time each night, including weekends.

questions.why: The article states that even with less blue light, stimulating content can still keep the brain awake.

wrong.A: Night mode reduces blue light; it does not make screens brighter.
wrong.C: The article does not say night mode turns devices off.
wrong.D: The article explains that blue light makes sleep harder.

questions.stem: A student sleeps nine hours on school nights but stays up until 3 a.m. on weekends. Based on the article, why might this be a problem?
options: Her routine is not consistent, which can confuse her body's internal clock
She is sleeping far too much on school nights
She will stop producing any growth hormone
Weekends do not count as part of the circadian rhythm
questions.why: The article stresses a consistent bedtime each night, and the circadian rhythm works as a daily clock, so large changes disrupt it.

wrong.B: Nine hours is within the recommended range.
wrong.C: The article does not say she would stop producing hormone completely.
wrong.D: The circadian rhythm works every day, including weekends.

questions.stem: In the article, a "sleep-deprived" student has trouble concentrating. What does sleep-deprived mean?
options: Having slept very deeply
Not having had enough sleep
Being afraid to sleep alone
Sleeping during lessons
questions.why: Deprived means lacking something, so a sleep-deprived student has not had enough sleep.

wrong.A: Deep sleep would help, not cause trouble concentrating.
wrong.C: The term is not about fear.
wrong.D: The term describes a lack of sleep, not where someone sleeps.

questions.stem: Why does the author describe sleep as one of the most productive periods for the body?
options: To argue that people should sleep during the day instead of at night, when screens are used
To show that sleep is boring compared with games
To challenge the idea that sleep is wasted time by listing what the body does
To explain how tablets are charged at night
questions.why: The author contrasts the common belief that sleep is wasted time with the growth, repair, memory, and immune work that happens during sleep.

wrong.A: The article does not suggest sleeping in the daytime instead.
wrong.B: The author argues the opposite: that sleep does important work.
wrong.D: Charging phones outside the room is advice, not the reason for this description.
